title: Setting Realistic Word Count Checkpoints for Your EE
summary: Build realistic EE word count checkpoints from September to November, with weekly targets, section budgets, recovery plans, and clear IB rule guidance.
body_markdown:
Setting realistic word count checkpoints means dividing your Extended Essay into complete, reviewable stages instead of attempting one late drafting push. From September to November, a sensible progression is approximately **1,000 words by mid-September, 2,000 by late September, 3,000 by mid-October, a complete draft by late October, and a revised 3,700-3,950-word version during November** .


These figures are planning recommendations, not official IB deadlines. Your school calendar takes priority, and your subject may require a different sequence. Effective checkpoints protect time for analysis, feedback, restructuring, and accurate referencing.


### Start with the official EE word limit


The IB describes the Extended Essay as an independent research project culminating in a paper of no more than **4,000 words** . This is a maximum, not a target that every essay must reach, and the IB does not prescribe monthly word totals.


The count normally includes the introduction, body, conclusion, quotations, and footnotes containing substantive discussion. The contents page, tables, equations, reference-only citations, bibliography, and reflection form are normally excluded. Confirm the rules in the guide for your examination session and follow any additional instructions from your school.


Students preparing for **first assessment in May 2027** use the revised framework described in the[official IB Extended Essay update](https://ibo.org/university-admission/latest-curriculum-updates/dp-extended-essay-updates/) . Earlier cohorts may use previous criteria, so always check which guide applies.


Word count is not a mark by itself. The[IB Extended Essay grade descriptors](https://ibo.org/contentassets/0b0b7a097ca2498ea50a9e41d9e1d1cf/dp-grade-descriptors-en.pdf) emphasize focus, evidence, analysis, evaluation, argument, and coherent presentation. A focused 3,850-word essay is stronger than a padded 4,000-word report.


### A realistic September-to-November checkpoint plan


This schedule assumes that September begins with a workable research question, preliminary evidence, and a basic outline.


Checkpoint Suggested cumulative count What should exist


Mid-September 800-1,200 words Introduction, approach, and one analytical section


End of September 1,800-2,200 words About half the argument, with citations


Mid-October 2,700-3,200 words Most body sections and relevant limitations


Late October 3,600-4,200 draft words Complete draft from introduction to conclusion


Mid-November 3,700-3,950 words Restructured version after feedback


Late November Within 4,000 words Proofread essay with checked references


A working draft may temporarily exceed 4,000 words while you compare explanations or evidence. The final submission must remain within the limit. The[RevisionDojo EE word count guide](https://www.revisiondojo.com/blog/mastering-the-ib-extended-essay-word-count-complete-guide-expert-tips) explains how to audit the count.


Each checkpoint should represent a **completed argument** , not disconnected notes. At 2,000 words, you should have multiple paragraphs containing claims, evidence, analysis, and links to the research question. Two thousand words of background information indicates less progress.


### Convert the total into a section budget


A provisional section budget prevents the introduction or context from consuming space needed for analysis.


Essay function Illustrative budget


Introduction and scope 300-450 words


Method, framework, or essential context 450-700 words


Main analysis and discussion 2,300-2,700 words


Conclusion and limitations 300-450 words


Editing buffer 150-250 words below the maximum


This is not an official template. Science essays may require more methodology and evaluation, while literature essays often integrate context into textual analysis. Use the[Extended Essay outline method](https://www.revisiondojo.com/blog/how-to-create-an-effective-ee-outline-for-a-logical-flow-step-by-step-ib-guide) to identify each section's claim, evidence, and analytical purpose before assigning words.


### Calculate targets from available sessions


Count the writing sessions you can realistically complete before your internal deadline. Exclude examination weeks, major IA deadlines, travel, and other known interruptions.

If you have 1,200 words and want a 3,800-word draft, you need another 2,600 words. Across ten sessions, that averages **260 words per session** . Some research-heavy sessions may produce only 150 polished words, while a well-planned analytical section may produce 500, so monitor the weekly total rather than judging every session equally.


### Match word count to draft quality


Every checkpoint needs a quality condition. Otherwise, numerical pressure encourages unnecessary context, long quotations, and repeated explanations.


At the end of each week, check that:


- every section helps answer the research question;
- claims are supported by cited evidence;
- evidence is followed by interpretation or evaluation;
- quotations are no longer than necessary;
- incomplete points are identified rather than concealed with filler;
- the bibliography is updated as you write.


The[guide to common EE mistakes](https://www.revisiondojo.com/blog/mistakes-to-avoid-in-ib-extended-essays) explains how excessive description, weak scope, and delayed citation work create misleading progress.


### Adjust checkpoints for your subject


Subject method affects when words can be produced. History, Literature, Economics, and Business Management students can often draft one argument while continuing targeted reading. In experimental sciences, incomplete data collection may prevent meaningful analysis.


Do not compensate for missing evidence by writing excessive theory. Replace a temporary word target with a concrete deliverable such as processing all trials, evaluating three primary sources, or completing a coding framework. Resume numerical targets once the evidence exists. Consult the IB's[subject-specific Extended Essay guidance](https://ibpublishing.ibo.org/extendedessay/apps/dpapp/guidance.html?doc=d_0_eeyyy_gui_1602_1_e) and RevisionDojo's[Extended Essay guides](https://www.revisiondojo.com/ee-guides) for subject-appropriate planning.


### Recover after missing a checkpoint


Missing one target is not solved by doubling the next day's workload. Diagnose whether the cause is insufficient evidence, an unstable question, an unclear outline, competing deadlines, or perfectionism.


Use three steps:


1. **Protect the argument.** Identify the sections essential to answering the question.
2. **Reduce the immediate target.** Schedule several manageable sessions instead of one catch-up block.
3. **Rebuild the calendar.** Move formatting later while preserving structural revision and supervisor feedback.


If you have 1,500 words at the start of October, aim for 2,100 by the first weekend, 2,700 by the second, and a rough complete draft by month-end. The[EE time-management guide](https://www.revisiondojo.com/blog/how-to-manage-time-efficiently-while-writing-your-ee-8-proven-ib-strategies) provides further scheduling strategies.


### Use feedback at the right checkpoint


Supervisor feedback is most useful when enough of the essay exists for its argument and structure to be assessed. Before submitting a formal draft, confirm what your supervisor expects and ask focused questions about method, evidence, balance, or reasoning.


After receiving comments, revise structure before polishing sentences. The[guide to improving an EE draft with feedback](https://www.revisiondojo.com/blog/how-to-improve-your-ib-extended-essay-draft-expert-feedback-guide) can help organize changes. Jojo AI may help identify whether a paragraph contains claim, evidence, and analysis, but all AI use must follow your school's academic integrity policy.


### Conclusion


Realistic EE word count checkpoints work when each number represents a genuine stage of the argument. Aim to move from about 1,000 words in mid-September to a complete draft in late October, then reserve November for restructuring, citations, tightening, and proofreading.


Treat these totals as adjustable planning tools rather than IB requirements. RevisionDojo's EE Support, Jojo AI, and Coursework Review can support specific drafting stages, but the best starting point is a section budget and regular protected writing sessions.
